name: R
title: R (4.5)

presenceList.meta: R1, Ec8, Ec9, D1, L1, G3, Q2, Q3

type.text: **Dynamic typing with no static check (T1)**: A value carries its type at run time, so a type error surfaces when the expression evaluates
**An atomic vector holds one type and coerces silently**: `c(1, "a")` becomes a character vector with no error, so a mixed vector changes type
**A factor stores integer level codes behind printed labels**: A comparison and an ordering can therefore differ from the text a reader sees

**`library()` copies a package's exported names onto the search path**: A package has its own namespace and `pkg::name` reaches any of its objects, but the habitual `library(pkg)` attaches the exports to the search path, so two packages that export one name collide and the later attachment masks the earlier
**A function is a first-class value with its own type**: `is.function`, `formals`, and `body` expose a function as data
**Attributes travel with a value invisibly**: A `names`, `class`, or `dim` attribute changes dispatch and printing, so two values that print alike can behave differently

construction.text: **A data frame is the central structured-data abstraction**: Named columns of one length form a table, and a model function accepts it without knowing how it was built

**Functions are first-class and an environment is a lexical home**: A function can be stored, passed, and returned, and it closes over its defining environment, so deliberate state is possible as a closure instead of a global
**The formula interface separates a model from a caller's data**: `y ~ x1 + x2` names the columns, so the same call works on any data frame that has them
**Global mutable state by default (C1)**: `<-` at top level writes into the global environment, and `<<-` writes into an enclosing environment, so a name is shared across the session
**No immutability by default (C2)**: A binding is assigned freely, and `attr(x, "a") <- v`, `names(x) <- v`, and a reference-class field change a value in place
**Many functions capture their arguments non-standardly**: `subset`, `with`, and most modelling functions evaluate an argument inside a data frame, so the call does not follow the usual rule

memory.text: **Copy-on-modify protects the reader**: A value is copied only when the copy is modified, so a function that receives a vector does not change the caller's value
**Copy-on-modify raises peak memory**: Modifying a large object can duplicate it, so the footprint exceeds the logical size of the data
**The collector runs on R's schedule (M2)**: Collection happens when R decides, and `gc()` reports heap use, but there is no block-scoped release
**No RAII (M3)**: There is no destructor at block exit, so a connection, a file, or a graphics device is closed by `on.exit` or explicitly
**No ownership model (M4)**: No static rule ties a value's storage to one binding
**`on.exit` registers exit-time cleanup**: An action runs when the function returns or raises, which is the R idiom for releasing a resource

**The undeclared class has no catch**: memory exhaustion at the allocator aborts the session (documented as the R-session crash), below the tryCatch surface (the nested-depth error is a catchable condition; the allocator abort is not)

error.text: **Conditions are classed objects**: `stop`, `warning`, and `message` signal a `condition` with a class, so a handler matches a class rather than a message string
**`tryCatch` separates recovery from cleanup**: An exiting handler returns a value, and `finally` runs on every path
**`withCallingHandlers` allows a non-unwinding response**: A handler can log a warning and let evaluation continue
**Unchecked exceptions only (Er2)**: A signalled condition propagates until something catches it, and no caller is required to handle it
**A warning is not an error**: It prints and evaluation continues, so an ignored warning can leave a wrong result
**No composable result value**: A failure is a thrown condition or a sentinel such as `NULL` or `NA`, so it does not compose through a call chain

concurrency.text: **`parallel` ships with the base distribution**: `mclapply` forks workers on Unix, and `makeCluster` with `parLapply` runs across sockets, so independent work splits without a shared-memory protocol
**A socket cluster passes results, not shared state**: A worker returns a value that is serialised back, so workers do not share an address space
**`future` and `%dopar%` give a declarative parallel surface**: Code written for a sequential `lapply` is unchanged when it runs in parallel
**Base R evaluates one expression at a time**: Vectorised operations are the usual substitute for a second thread
**A forked worker copies on write**: `mclapply` shares the parent's memory until a worker modifies it, and then it duplicates
**Reproducibility needs explicit seed handling**: A parallel random stream requires `clusterSetRNGStream` or the `future` seed mechanism

platform.text: **One open-source implementation with several distributors**: The R Core Team maintains the interpreter under the GNU GPL, and CRAN ships source and binaries
**Official builds cover the three desktop platforms**: Linux, macOS, and Windows binaries are published for each release
**The interpreter is not tied to one editor**: RStudio, VS Code, Emacs ESS, and the plain console drive the same R
**Package installation is declarative**: `install.packages` fetches from a named mirror, and `renv` records exact versions in a lockfile
**A source package with C or C++ needs a toolchain**: The published binary avoids the compiler, but a source install needs headers and a linker

performance.text: **Vectorised and matrix operations call compiled C, C++, and BLAS/LAPACK code**: `colSums`, `%*%`, and `lm` do their work in compiled libraries, so the interpreter is not in the inner loop
**A large set of compiled packages exists**: `data.table`, `Rcpp`, and `Matrix` move hot paths into compiled code, and CRAN distributes them
**Interpreted with no ahead-of-time compilation (R1)**: Base R executes an interpreted form, so a scalar loop is slower than its compiled equivalent
**The just-in-time compiler helps only where it applies**: The byte-code compiler (level 3, `cmpfun`) speeds up a loop, but the gain is bounded
**Memory pressure shows up as time**: Copying and collection cost time that the source does not show

ecosystem.text: **CRAN is a large, curated, central repository**: Tens of thousands of packages pass an automated check before publication
**The RStudio IDE is a first-class environment**: Console, source editor, plots, and a debugger sit in one window
**Reproducibility tooling is mature**: `renv` records a project library, and a package manager can pin a date-based snapshot
**Package quality varies**: The CRAN check verifies correctness and portability, not statistical validity, so a method needs its own reading
**A deployment needs the full environment**: R, a build toolchain, and system libraries for compiled dependencies make a project heavier to ship than a single binary
**Binaries bind to an R major release**: R 4.0.0 required every package to be reinstalled, and the C API manual promises notice, not binary stability [@rNews; @rExtApi]

**Stored workspaces bind to the release**: serialization format 3 is the default since R 3.6.0, R states that format-3 data cannot be read by versions prior to 3.5.0, and version = 2 is the documented way to write a file an older R opens [@rNewsSerialization]

evolution.text: **Backward compatibility is strong and documented**: The Core Team publishes a `NEWS` file per release and keeps the language API stable, so an old script generally still runs
**A regular release cadence exists**: An x.y.0 release appears each spring and a patch release follows in the same year
**The tidyverse and r-lib provide deprecation discipline**: The `lifecycle` package marks a function as experimental, deprecated, or superseded before removal
**A third-party package can break across a major release**: A package that used an internal API can fail after an upgrade, and the fix belongs to its maintainer
**A package can be archived from CRAN**: An unmaintained package is removed from the index, so code that depends on it needs a replacement or a frozen snapshot

domain.text: **Excellent fit for statistical computing**: `lm`, `glm`, `aov`, and `t.test` are in the base distribution with a formula interface
**CRAN and Bioconductor cover the applied fields**: Biostatistics, econometrics, time series, and genomics each have dedicated packages
**A report is generated from the analysis itself**: `knitr`, `rmarkdown`, and Quarto run the code and place its output in the document
**Domain lock-in to statistics and data analysis (D1)**: The core value types, the formula interface, and the modelling packages assume a data-analysis workflow
**A production service in R is unusual**: A service with a high request rate is usually written elsewhere and calls R for the model

learning.text: **Steep (L1)**: The idioms — vectorisation, the apply family, environments, and S3 dispatch — take time for a programmer from an imperative language
**Non-standard evaluation surprises newcomers**: An argument can be evaluated inside a data frame, so `subset` and `dplyr` code does not follow the usual call rule
**Factor semantics are unfamiliar**: A factor compares by its integer level code, so an ordering or a comparison can differ from the printed text
**The apply family is confusing**: `sapply` varies its return type with the input, so a result is not predictable from the call alone
**Documentation is generated, complete, and mandated**: Every CRAN package must document every exported function, and `?` reaches the reference page

syntax.text: **The formula interface and the pipe are compact**: `y ~ x` and `x |> f()` read as a data pipeline
**Indexing follows one rule across atomic, list, and data-frame values**: `[`, `[[`, and `$` behave consistently, so a new structure needs no new syntax
**Two assignment operators exist**: `<-` binds a name in the current environment, and `=` also assigns at top level but separates a named argument inside a call, so the meaning depends on position
**`.` is overloaded**: It means every other variable in a formula and the piped value in a magrittr pipe
**A print method hides structure**: Printing a data frame or a model object shows a summary, so `str()` is needed to see the actual shape

testing.text: **`testthat` is the de facto standard framework**: It provides expectations, a runner, and a per-file test structure
**A package must pass `R CMD check`**: CRAN runs the check, which executes the tests and the examples, so a package is not published with a failing test
**Property-based and snapshot testing exist**: `hedgehog` generates inputs, and a `testthat` snapshot records output for comparison
**Interactive debugging is available**: `browser()`, `traceback()`, `debug()`, and the RStudio debugger stop at a line and inspect its environment
**Errors are runtime-only (G3)**: A type error appears when the line runs, so the test suite is what reaches the untested path
**A suite depends on the installed environment**: The tests run through the package machinery, so the environment must be installed first

security.text: **Known vulnerability/injection (Q3)**: `eval(parse(text = ...))`, `do.call` on a string, and `system()` turn text into code or a command, so concatenated input is an injection surface
**Dynamic typing carries its risk into security code**: A check written for one class can pass an object of another class, and dispatch then runs a different method
**`system2` reduces but does not remove shell risk**: It passes arguments as a vector, yet a shell is still involved
**`load` and `readRDS` restore an object, not only data**: A serialised object can carry an environment, so restoring untrusted state is a code-execution path
**The interpreter runs with the user's full privileges**: R has no sandbox of its own, so code in a session has the user's access to files and the network
**CRAN policy limits what a package may do**: Network access and writes outside the temporary directory are restricted during install and check

governance.text: **Semantics rest on the reference implementation**: the language definition enumerates some unspecified behavior, and no conformance suite exists for an independent implementation to run

tradeoffs: **Copy-on-modify is a deliberate trade**: Immutability by copy protects callers and costs peak memory

**Non-standard evaluation is a deliberate design**: It makes `subset(d, x > 1)` and a formula interface readable and lets a modelling call record the variable names it was given, at the cost of evaluation that is not visible at the call site
**The global environment is for interactive analysis**: A session-wide namespace suits exploratory work at the console
**A factor encodes categorical data**: The hidden integer code is the price of ordered levels and of a compact representation
**One-based indexing and `<-` are convention choices**: They follow the S language and the statistics literature, so the cost is familiarity, not a forced dependency
**R is for statistics, not general programming**: The assumption of a data-analysis workload is a scope decision
verdict: R's design yields moderate coupling for statistical computing and higher coupling outside it. Vectorised operations and compiled linear algebra remove per-element iteration from the source, and the formula interface separates a model from a caller's data. Main strengths: a curated package ecosystem, first-class functions and environments, and a strong fit for data analysis. Main weaknesses: dynamic typing with no static check, the global environment as the default destination of `<-`, copy-on-modify memory cost, non-standard evaluation that hides where an argument is evaluated, a steep learning curve, and dynamic code paths (`eval`, `system`) that carry injection risk.

energy.text: Interpreted by default: the slowest class in the energy and time benchmarks [@pereira2017energy]; a causal re-analysis attributes most of the gap to execution time [@vankempen2025green].

ai-readiness.text: Moderate training data: models write it competently, with measurable language-specific weakness [@joel2025lowresource].

safety.text: No certified or standards-qualified path for safety-critical systems.

delivery.note: A source package builds on the target machine
R 4.0.0 requires every package to be reinstalled under that release, and the C API manual promises notice, not binary stability

data_formats.note: R states that serialized data in serialization format 3, the default for save(), serialize(), and saveRDS() since R 3.6.0, cannot be read by versions of R prior to 3.5.0, and points to the version = 2 option that restores the older format
